addedResources.name: PyTorch 2.14 numerical accuracy and tensor testing
addedResources.use: Read the numerical-accuracy introduction, Extremal values, non-finite inputs and Ampere precision sections, plus the assert_close contract and make_tensor parameters. These supply current comparison semantics missing from the pool's project checklist.

addedResources.name: CUDA 13.4 Floating Point and IEEE 754
addedResources.use: Read sections 2.2, 3.1 to 3.2 and 4.4 for reduction order and single-precision flush-to-zero flags. Do not use the historical CPU-has-no-FMA statements as current hardware facts.

units.title: Timed boundaries, asynchronous launch and event timing
outcomes: Define a timed boundary that separates kernel execution, host dispatch, transfers and setup.
Measure completed work with stream-ordered events and a synchronized host timer.
Repair a launch-only timing claim and explain any remaining timer disagreement.
units.why: A host call can return before its GPU work finishes. A speedup is meaningful only when both variants time the same completed work.

next.note: Separate first-use costs from steady-state execution.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 2: end-to-end benchmarking
study.locator: Section 2.1.3, End-to-End Benchmarking, and Problem (benchmarking_script), parts (a) and (b), pp. 3 to 4

study.title: Companion code: event-timed coalesced copy
study.locator: Commit b57e4c6: `coalesced_stream`, then `main` from allocation through event destruction
study.depth: Read the timing sequence. Do not treat its average over 40 launches as a distribution of individual-call latency.

focus: Write the benchmark question first: isolated kernel time, completed operator latency, or end-to-end step time. Name every included and excluded cost.
Record start and stop events on the work's stream, then wait for the stop event before reading elapsed time. Other streams need explicit dependencies.
For host wall time, complete prior work before starting and included work before stopping. Validation and input generation stay outside a kernel-only interval.
An event interval can include GPU idle gaps while the host supplies launches. Dividing a batch interval by its launch count measures amortized service time, not a latency percentile.
units.reproduce: Allocate two seeded 512 by 512 `torch.float32` CUDA matrices. Warm up 10 matrix multiplies, synchronize, then time 20 multiplies with events and with a host timer spanning the same batch and final synchronization. Validate the last output against a CPU double-precision reference. Explain the two boundaries without assuming equal times or a fixed speedup.
traps: Timing only the return from `torch.matmul` and calling that kernel duration.
Recording events on the default stream while the measured work runs on another stream.
Calling `.item()` inside the loop and accidentally including a device-to-host synchronization.

selfTest.q: Why synchronize before starting a host timer as well as after the work?
selfTest.a: The first wait excludes queued earlier work. The final wait includes completion of the work being measured.

selfTest.q: Does waiting for a stop event prove all device work has completed?
selfTest.a: Only work ordered before that event, including explicit dependencies. Unrelated streams can still be running.

selfTest.q: Why can a batch event interval exceed the sum of kernel durations in a trace?
selfTest.a: The interval includes time between its event timestamps, including launch-supply gaps and interference. Kernel durations alone exclude those gaps.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `benchmarking_script` (a) and (b)
practice.note: Use batch 1, context 128, width 128, feed-forward width 512, 2 layers, 4 heads and vocabulary 1,024 as a starting configuration for a 6 GB GPU. Reduce further if needed and record all changes. Time forward-only and training separately. These are written deliverables, not public timing tests; add your own correctness checks.

units.stopWhen: Your harness reports both completed host latency and event time with explicit boundaries, validates the output, and rejects an unsynchronized launch-only result as a kernel-time claim.

fit.note: The assignment explains asynchronous timing; the pinned copy example supplies the event sequence, and the named benchmarking problem provides practice.

units.title: Warmup, compilation, allocator and cache state
outcomes: Separate compilation, autotuning and allocator initialization from warm execution.
Choose and record an application-relevant cache and buffer-reuse policy.
Use a bounded warmup rule and retain evidence when steady state does not settle.
units.why: First-use overhead and repeated-buffer reuse answer different questions from steady-state work on changing inputs. Neither should silently enter the other result.

next.note: Check whether apparent warmup is actually clock or thermal drift.

study.title: CUTLASS: warmup and buffer rotation
study.locator: Documentation updated September 21, 2026: Benchmark Requirements; Warm-ups and Profiling Iterations; Buffer Rotation
study.depth: Do not copy the Blackwell iteration counts. The claim that rotation guarantees DRAM-resident inputs is too strong: replacement, access coverage and persistence affect residency. Treat rotation as an eviction strategy to check, not proof of a cold cache.

study.title: Allocator pools versus data caches
study.locator: Chapter 6, CUDA Programming Refresher: Asynchronous Memory Allocation and Memory Pools

study.title: Harness cold and warm contract
study.locator: Architecture constraints; Milestone B - Instrumentation, compilation/autotuning and cold/warm items

focus: A warmed allocator, compiled code cache, tuned configuration, L2 cache and application KV cache are different state. Record them separately.
Warm every evaluated shape, dtype and specialization. A new shape can trigger compilation or tuning after another shape has settled.
Inspect warmup batches and clock state with a declared stability rule and a time cap. A fixed count is not evidence of convergence.
Reuse buffers when reuse represents the application. Rotate preallocated buffers when studying streaming traffic; exclude rotation setup and label unverified residency.
units.reproduce: From a fresh process, record the first call and subsequent batches for the timing unit's matrix multiply. Repeat with preallocated rotating inputs and with the same inputs reused. Keep the warmup samples and declare which state each run preserves. Do not require a difference: a small workload or unchanged execution path may show none.
traps: Calling `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` between trials and claiming to have flushed L2. It releases unused allocator cache, not a hardware data cache.
Putting compilation or input allocation in only one variant's timed boundary.
Running warmup forever to obtain a preferred timing while hiding thermal drift.

selfTest.q: Does a warm model imply every specialization is compiled?
selfTest.a: No. New shapes, dtypes or guards can create new specializations or trigger tuning.

selfTest.q: Is repeated-buffer caching always a benchmark defect?
selfTest.a: No. It is legitimate when the target workload reuses those buffers. It is misleading when presented as streaming DRAM performance.

selfTest.q: Why keep a first-call result even when reporting warm performance?
selfTest.a: It exposes startup, compilation and tuning costs that warm timing deliberately excludes. Deployment may pay them.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `benchmarking_script` (c)
practice.note: Reuse the reduced model from the timing unit. Compare zero, one, two and five warmup steps, then test your bounded stability rule. Keep identical timed boundaries and record allocator and specialization state. The section mini-project adds the rotating-buffer cache experiment.

units.stopWhen: You can regenerate separate first-use and warm reports with retained warmup samples, a bounded stability rule, and an explicit allocator and buffer-reuse policy.

fit.note: CUTLASS, the allocator section and the project contract cover the state distinctions; assignment part (c) gives named warmup practice.

units.title: Clocks, power, interference and environment capture
outcomes: Capture hardware, software, build and workload identity alongside raw samples.
Identify power, thermal, clock and background-work changes that weaken a comparison.
Measure under a documented isolation policy without assuming an idle process list proves isolation.
units.why: Laptop clocks and shared-device activity can change during a benchmark. The environment is part of the result, not an optional appendix.

next.note: Make comparisons robust to remaining time-dependent noise.

study.title: CUTLASS: environment and data-dependent power
study.locator: Documentation updated September 21, 2026: Testing Methodology Overview and Matrix Fill Methodology
study.depth: Read fixed-frequency tests as a controlled methodology, not an instruction to change shared-machine clocks. Zero-filled inputs are not a representative default, even with a frequency setting.

study.title: Machine and build identity
study.locator: Core requirements, harness item; Failure-injection requirements, thermal/interference run; Measurement requirements; Rubric, Reproducibility

focus: Record GPU identity and compute capability, driver, toolkit, framework and compiler versions, flags, code revision, workload seed and precision settings. Driver-supported CUDA and the installed toolkit are not the same version.
Save sampled clocks, power and temperature with trial timestamps. Missing or unsupported telemetry must be marked unavailable, not zero.
On the shared laptop, serialize experiments with the shared lock, keep them short and release allocations on exit. Desktop activity remains outside that lock.
Compare identical input distributions. Fill patterns can change switching activity and power; a fixed power limit does not imply fixed clocks.
units.reproduce: Attach a machine/build manifest and timestamped clock, power and temperature observations to one short timing run. Record background processes and whether clocks can be controlled without privileges. Repeat the same run later with interleaved variants; explain any state differences without attributing every fluctuation to a single cause.
traps: Using `nvidia-smi`'s displayed CUDA support level as the compiler version.
Assuming the shared lock blocks the desktop or users who do not take the lock.
Deleting slow samples after seeing a thermal or interference event instead of preserving and labeling the affected run.

selfTest.q: Does a fixed power limit make two runs use the same clock?
selfTest.a: No. Dynamic voltage and frequency control responds to temperature, workload and power demand. Measure clocks during the run.

selfTest.q: Why is recording only the GPU model insufficient?
selfTest.a: Driver, compiler, libraries, flags, power state and workload can all change the generated work or its runtime.

selfTest.q: What can you claim when power telemetry is unavailable?
selfTest.a: Timing and the state you actually observed. You cannot infer an energy result or rule out power effects from missing readings.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` environment manifest, timestamped machine-state log and interference/isolation audit.
units.stopWhen: A retained raw run can be matched to its workload, revision, toolchain, machine-state observations and stated isolation limits without relying on memory.

fit.note: CUTLASS supplies clock, power and fill guidance; the project defines environment capture and the mini-project provides the manifest audit.

units.title: Interleaved trials, raw samples and uncertainty
outcomes: Collect paired, interleaved trials with reproducible randomized order and raw samples.
Report medians, supported tails and uncertainty without treating launches within a batch as independent trials.
Separate statistical evidence from a practically worthwhile improvement.
units.why: A best timing hides drift and noise. Paired trials make a comparison less dependent on which variant happened to run first.

study.title: Harness noise and repeated-trial requirements
study.locator: Core requirements, harness item; Milestone B - Instrumentation, noise and observer overhead; Milestone E - Measurement / optimization, interleaved raw trials; Measurement requirements

study.title: CS336: repeated timing summary
study.locator: Section 2.1.3, Problem (benchmarking_script), part (b), p. 4
study.depth: Use its mean and standard deviation as an initial summary. Ten steps do not establish a reliable p99 or confidence interval under time-correlated drift.

focus: Make a trial pair use identical inputs and timing boundaries. Randomize the order within each pair with a recorded seed and preserve timestamps.
Report the estimand: ratio of medians and median paired ratio are different statistics. Keep raw times, not just speedups.
Resample whole pairs for paired uncertainty. If adjacent pairs drift together, use blocks or repeated sessions rather than an independent-sample bootstrap.
State sample count, percentile convention and a minimum useful gain before inspecting results. Tail estimates need many independent observations, not many launches inside one interval.
units.reproduce: Using synthetic paired latencies in milliseconds, baseline `[10, 20, 30]` and candidate `[5, 10, 15]`, compute both medians and each paired speedup. Both summaries give a speedup of 2. Explain why resampling these perfectly proportional pairs can produce zero spread without proving a noise-free hardware result. Then compute the same summaries on retained interleaved GPU samples.
traps: Running all baseline trials before all candidate trials and confounding the variant with clock drift.
Treating 1,000 launches in one event interval as 1,000 independent latency samples.
Reporting a confidence interval without its resampling unit or treating a tiny statistically resolved gain as automatically useful.

selfTest.q: Why randomize within a pair rather than always run baseline first?
selfTest.a: It reduces systematic order effects. Pairing limits slow drift, but randomization does not eliminate carryover or all interference.

selfTest.q: What is lost when only medians are retained?
selfTest.a: Tails, outliers, order effects and information needed to recompute uncertainty or change the summary.

selfTest.q: Does a p99 computed from ten trials give strong tail evidence?
selfTest.a: No. It is effectively an estimate near the sample maximum, with very poor information about rare slow events.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: `kernellab` paired randomized trials, raw samples, drift plots and a documented uncertainty calculation.
units.stopWhen: Your report can be regenerated from raw paired trials and states the summary statistic, uncertainty method, dependence limits and minimum practically useful gain.

fit.note: The project explicitly requires interleaving, uncertainty and noise characterization; CS336 supplies the starting repeated-trial task, extended in the mini-project.

units.title: Independent references and differential and property tests
outcomes: Build a reference that does not reuse the target's indexing or reduction logic.
Test supported shapes, strides, dtypes and masks, including boundaries and invalid inputs.
Gate every performance result on differential and property checks.
units.why: A faster kernel that computes the wrong operation is not an optimization. Independent references and adversarial properties catch errors that two similar implementations share.

next.note: Turn numerical agreement into an explicit acceptance contract.

study.title: Independent oracle and adversarial matrix
study.locator: Architecture constraints; Milestone A - Correct baseline; Correctness requirements; Failure-injection requirements

study.title: PyTorch 2.14: test inputs and structural comparison
study.locator: `torch.testing.assert_close`: shape, device, dtype, layout and stride checks; `torch.testing.make_tensor`: shape, range and noncontiguous parameters

focus: Generate reference results from the specification using a CPU scalar or library path, not the target's address calculations. Use the same represented inputs.
Include empty, singleton, odd, warp-edge and block-edge sizes; noncontiguous views; supported dtypes; and partial or all-masked rows. Unsupported combinations must reject or fall back explicitly.

Properties complement an oracle: copies preserve each element, transposing twice restores the input, and finite nonempty softmax rows sum approximately to one. These properties alone do not identify every wrong output.
Preserve seeds and failing inputs. Check output shape, dtype and required layout as well as values, with tolerances chosen before tuning.
units.reproduce: Write a copy acceptance test for lengths 0, 1, 31, 32, 33, 255, 256 and 257. Use a stride-two view of a known sequence, then compare every output element with an independently indexed CPU reference at zero tolerance. Verify that a deliberately omitted last element fails and that the empty-input path avoids an invalid zero-block launch.
traps: Sharing a stride calculation between the oracle and candidate, so both make the same indexing mistake.
Comparing only sums or checksums. Permutations and compensating errors can preserve them.
Silently making noncontiguous inputs contiguous before testing a path advertised as stride-aware.

selfTest.q: Can the transpose-twice property prove a transpose implementation is correct?
selfTest.a: No. Even an identity operation passes it. Compare against an independent transpose reference as well.

selfTest.q: Why test just above a block boundary?
selfTest.a: It forces a partial final block and exposes tail guards, skipped elements and out-of-bounds accesses.

selfTest.q: Should a contiguous-only kernel pass a strided input by ignoring its strides?
selfTest.a: No. It must reject, use a correct fallback, or perform a declared layout conversion whose cost is included at the operator boundary.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: `kernellab` independent copy/reduction references, adversarial input matrix and seeded tail/stride regressions.
units.stopWhen: Your supported-input matrix passes independent full-output checks, and seeded tail and stride defects fail before the harness publishes timing results.

fit.note: The project supplies the reference and property-test requirements, but lacks current tensor comparison APIs. PyTorch 2.14 testing documentation closes that implementation gap.

units.title: Tolerances and an extreme-value policy
outcomes: Derive an absolute-plus-relative acceptance rule and justify its scale from precision, reduction order and output use.
Separate input rounding from accumulation error using a higher-precision reference.
Declare and test policies for non-finite inputs, masked rows, overflow, underflow and subnormals.
units.why: Floating-point order changes can be legitimate, but a loose tolerance can conceal a defect. Extreme values need semantic decisions, not a larger error threshold.

next.note: Use the contract when reduction order changes.

study.title: CS336: accumulation precision experiment
study.locator: Section 2.1.5, Problem (mixed_precision_accumulation), pp. 7 to 8

study.title: PyTorch 2.14: numerical limits
study.locator: Introduction; Extremal values; Linear algebra - Non-finite values and Extremal values in linalg; TensorFloat-32 on Nvidia Ampere; Reduced Precision Reduction for FP16 and BF16 GEMMs
study.depth: Skip the slice example: `A.sum(-1)[0]` and `A[:,0].sum()` are different mathematical sums. Do not use that example as evidence of rounding differences. Skip the AMD-specific sections.

study.title: Finite and non-finite comparison rules
study.locator: `torch.testing.assert_close`: closeness inequality, non-finite comparison and `rtol`, `atol`, `equal_nan` parameters

study.title: CUDA 13.4: order and subnormal controls
study.locator: Sections 2.2, Operations and Accuracy; 3.1 to 3.2, dot-product algorithms and comparison; 4.4, Compiler Flags

focus: For finite outputs use \(|y-\hat y| \le a+r|\hat y|\), where \(\hat y\) is the reference and \(a\) and \(r\) are declared absolute and relative tolerances. Near zero, relative error alone is unsuitable.
Evaluate quantized inputs in higher precision to isolate accumulation error. Comparing with unrounded original inputs adds input-representation error to the result.
Cancellation and ill-conditioning can amplify relative error. A dtype-only default is not an error bound for arbitrary reduction lengths or applications.
Test NaN and infinity locations separately. Declare all-masked-row behavior, overflow handling and subnormal preservation or flushing; record precision modes and compiler flags.
units.reproduce: Run the four CS336 accumulation loops unchanged on CPU. In PyTorch 2.14.1, the FP32 loop gives 10.000133514404297 and the FP16 loop gives 9.953125; both loops with FP16 increments accumulated in FP32 give 10.00213623046875. Explain input rounding versus repeated accumulation rounding, then define acceptance and extreme-input policies for your reduction. These are numerical examples, not GPU timing results.
traps: Increasing tolerance until an omitted element or wrong mask passes.
Setting `equal_nan=True` and calling unexpected NaNs correct.
Assuming max-subtracted softmax defines an all-masked row. Subtracting negative infinity from itself produces NaN; the application must specify a separate policy.

selfTest.q: Why does promoting a rounded FP16 increment to FP32 not recover the original decimal value?
selfTest.a: Promotion preserves the already rounded value. It improves subsequent accumulation, not the information lost on conversion.

selfTest.q: Can a finite final mathematical answer guarantee finite intermediate arithmetic?
selfTest.a: No. Intermediate products, squares or sums can overflow even when a rearranged or higher-precision calculation has a representable final answer.

selfTest.q: Does a larger relative tolerance repair comparison near a zero reference?
selfTest.a: No. The relative term vanishes at zero. Use a justified absolute tolerance and investigate cancellation.

selfTest.q: What does `-ftz=true` change for single-precision CUDA arithmetic?
selfTest.a: It enables flushing subnormal values to zero in affected operations. Record it as a numerical-semantic choice, not just a performance flag.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `mixed_precision_accumulation`
practice.note: Run all four loops and explain each discrepancy from the real-arithmetic sum of 10. This written experiment has no public autograder. The section mini-project adds cancellation, NaN, infinity, overflow, underflow and all-masked policy tests.

units.stopWhen: You explain all four accumulation results and defend a predeclared finite-output tolerance plus separate extreme-value policies that reject a seeded wrong-mask or skipped-element defect.

fit.note: CS336 covers accumulation practice but not the full current comparison and extreme-value contract. PyTorch 2.14 and CUDA 13.4 close those coverage and currency gaps.
